etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English helle, from Old English hell, from Proto-West Germanic *hallju, from Proto-Germanic *haljō (“concealed place, netherworld”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to cover, conceal, save”).

Cognate with Saterland Frisian Hälle (“hell”), West Frisian hel (“hell”), Dutch hel (“hell”), German Low German Hell (“hell”), German Hölle (“hell”), Norwegian helvete (“hell”), Icelandic hel (“the abode of the dead, death”). Also related to the Hel of Germanic mythology. See also hele.

definitions.definition: (countable, hyperbolic, figuratively) A place or situation of great suffering in life.

quote.citation: 1879, General William T. Sherman, commencement address at the Michigan Military Academy
quote.text: There is many a boy here today who looks on war as all glory, but, boys, it is all hell.

quote.citation: 1986, “Disposable Heroes”, in Metallica (music), Master of Puppets:
quote.text: Why, am I dying? / Kill, have no fear / Lie, live off lying / Hell, hell is here

quote.citation: 2024 May 8, Damian Carrington, “‘Hopeless and broken’: why the world’s top climate scientists are in despair.   World’s top climate scientists expect global heating to blast past 1.5C target”, in The Guardian, UK:
quote.text: So how do the scientists cope with their work being ignored for decades, and living in a world their findings indicate is on a “highway to hell”?.

quote.citation: 1848 November – 1850 December, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 61, in The History of Pendennis. […], volume (please specify |volume=I or II), London: Bradbury and Evans, […], published 1849–1850, →OCLC:
quote.text: Here’s five-and-twenty for you. Don’t be losing it at the hells now.

quote.citation: 1877, William Black, Green Pastures and Piccadilly:
quote.text: a convenient little gambling hell for those who had grown reckless

quote.citation: 1906 January–October, Joseph Conrad, chapter II, in The Secret Agent: A Simple Tale, London: Methuen & Co., […], published 1907, →OCLC;  The Secret Agent: A Simple Tale (Collection of British Authors; 3995), copyright edition, Leipzig: Bernhard Tauchnitz, 1907, →OCLC, page 15:
quote.text: But there was also about him an indescribable air which no mechanic could have acquired in the practice of his handicraft however dishonestly exercised: [...] the air of moral nihilism common to keepers of gambling hells and disorderly houses; [...]

definitions.definition: (sometimes vulgar) Used as an intensifier in phrases grammatically requiring a noun.
(obsolete) A place into which a tailor throws shreds, or a printer discards broken type.

quote.citation: 1662 (indicated as 1663), [Samuel Butler], “[The First Part of Hudibras]”, in Hudibras. The First and Second Parts. […], London:  […]  John Martyn and Henry Herringman, […], published 1678; republished in A[lfred] R[ayney] Waller, editor, Hudibras: Written in the Time of the Late Wars, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire: University Press, 1905, →OCLC:
quote.text: This sturdy Squire, he had, as well As the bold Trojan Knight, seen Hell.

definitions.definition: In certain games of chase, a place to which those who are caught are carried for detention.
(colloquial, usually with on) Something extremely painful or harmful (to)
(colloquial, sometimes vulgar) Used to express discontent, unhappiness, or anger.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene vii]:
quote.text: O hell! what have we here?A carrion Death, within whose empty eyeThere is a written scroll!  […]

definitions.definition: (colloquial, sometimes vulgar, non-productive) Used to emphasize.
(colloquial, sometimes vulgar) Used to introduce an intensified statement following an understated one; nay; not only that, but.
(postpositional) Alternative form of the hell or like hell.

quote.citation: 1991 September, Stephen Fry, chapter 1, in The Liar, London: Heinemann, →ISBN, →OCLC, section II, page 24:
quote.text: ‘[…]  I know whether a boy is telling me the truth or not.’‘Thank you, sir.’Did he hell. They never bloody did.

definitions.definition: (Australia, New Zealand, colloquial, sometimes vulgar) Very; used to emphasize strongly.
To make hellish; to place (someone) in hell; to make (a place) into a hell. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1929, William Faulkner, The Sound and the Fury:
quote.text: I had already lost thirteen points, all because she had to come helling in there at twelve, worrying me about that letter.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To move quickly and loudly; to raise hell as part of motion.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From German hellen (“to brighten, burnish”). Related to Dutch hel (“clear, bright”) and German hell (“clear, bright”).

definitions.definition: (rare, metal-working) To add luster to; to burnish (silver or gold).

quote.citation: 1770, Godfrey Smith, The Laboratory: Or, School of Arts:
quote.text: To hell gold or gilt workː take two ounces of tartar, two ounces of sulfur.. and it will give it a fine luster.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hellen, from Old Norse hella (“to pour”), from Proto-Germanic *halþijaną (“to incline, tip; to pour out, empty”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to lean, incline”). Cognate with Icelandic hella (“to pour”), Norwegian helle (“to pour”), Swedish hälla (“to pour”). See also English hield.

quote.citation: 18th century, Josiah Relph, The Harvest; or Bashful Shepherd
quote.text: Gosh, the sickle went into me handː Down hell'd the bluid.
